topic: Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A sealed flask contains 4.0 g of helium gas, He (Ar = 4). Which sample of methane gas, CH4 (Mr = 16), occupies the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure?
items.why: Particle diagrams of solids and liquids show particles touching, so students picture gas molecules as packed together and conclude that bigger molecules need a bigger box. In a gas the molecules are far apart, and the space between them rather than their own size sets the volume, so one mole of any gas occupies the same volume under the same conditions.

items.q: Two gas syringes are held at the same temperature and pressure. One contains 0.50 mol of nitrogen, N2 (Mr = 28), and the other contains 0.50 mol of sulfur dioxide, SO2 (Mr = 64). Which statement about the two gas volumes is correct?
items.correct: The two volumes are the same, because the amounts in moles are equal.
items.misconception: The sulfur dioxide has the larger volume, as its molecules are heavier.
items.why: Particle diagrams of solids and liquids show particles touching, so students picture gas molecules as packed together and conclude that bigger molecules need a bigger box. In a gas the molecules are far apart, and the space between them rather than their own size sets the volume, so one mole of any gas occupies the same volume under the same conditions.
items.random_wrong: The nitrogen has the smaller volume, as it is the lighter gas here.

items.q: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure)?
items.why: 22.4 dm³ is the molar volume at 0 °C and 1 atmosphere and appears in many textbooks and online sources, so it is recalled in place of the value this specification gives for room temperature and pressure. This specification uses room temperature and pressure, 20 °C and 1 atmosphere, at which the volume of one mole of any gas is 24 dm³.

items.q: A balloon holds 3.0 mol of argon gas at room temperature and pressure. What is the volume of the gas in the balloon?
items.why: Most mole calculations students have met involve dividing (mass ÷ Mr, moles ÷ volume for concentration), so dividing becomes the default move whenever 24 appears. One mole occupies 24 dm³, so more moles means more volume: volume (dm³) = amount (mol) × 24. Dividing would make a larger amount of gas give a smaller volume.

items.q: A sample of carbon dioxide gas, CO2 (Mr = 44), has a mass of 8.8 g. What is the volume of this sample at room temperature and pressure?
items.why: The rule 'volume = amount × 24' is remembered as 'volume = number × 24', and the only number in the question is the mass, so the mass is used in place of the amount. Only an amount in moles may be multiplied by 24. Convert first: 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol, then 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³.

items.q: What is the volume of 4.0 g of oxygen gas, O2, at room temperature and pressure? (Ar of O = 16)
items.why: The periodic table gives the relative atomic mass of the atom, and students take that number without checking the formula of the substance, which for oxygen gas is O2. Use the formula of the substance as it appears in the equation. Oxygen gas is O2, so Mr = 2 × 16 = 32.

items.q: At room temperature and pressure, volume (dm³) = amount of substance (mol) × 24. A student has measured the volume of a gas in dm³ and wants the amount in moles. Which step gives the amount in moles?
items.correct: Divide the volume in dm³ by 24.
items.misconception: Subtract 24 from the volume in dm³.
items.why: Rearranging is remembered as 'move it across and change the sign', a rule learned for equations built by addition, and it is then applied to an equation built by multiplication. A quantity that multiplies on one side divides on the other. Since volume = amount × 24, dividing both sides by 24 gives amount = volume ÷ 24.
items.random_wrong: Multiply the volume in dm³ by 24.

items.q: For a gas at room temperature and pressure, volume (dm³) = (mass (g) ÷ Mr) × 24. A student knows the volume and the Mr of the gas and wants its mass. Which pair of steps gives the mass?
items.correct: Multiply the volume by the Mr, and then divide by 24.
items.misconception: Multiply the volume by 24, then divide by the Mr.
items.why: The two steps are undone in one move rather than one at a time, so a quantity that was dividing is left dividing instead of being brought up to multiply. Undo one step at a time. Multiply both sides by Mr, then divide by 24: mass = volume × Mr ÷ 24.
items.random_wrong: Divide the volume by the Mr, then divide by 24.

items.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). A student wants to use this equation to work out gas volumes at room temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Only the carbon dioxide has a gas volume here.
items.misconception: Every substance shown occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
items.why: The rule 'one mole occupies 24 dm³' is remembered without the word 'gas', so it is applied to any substance in the equation whatever its state symbol. The molar volume of 24 dm³ applies to gases only. Read the state symbols and include only species labelled (g).
items.random_wrong: The calcium oxide also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.

items.q: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 30 cm³ of nitrogen reacts completely with excess hydrogen. What volume of ammonia is formed, measured at the same temperature and pressure?
items.why: The molar volume is the most memorable item in the topic, so 24 is inserted into every gas calculation whether or not a mass or an amount in moles is involved. Equal amounts in moles occupy equal volumes, so for gases at the same conditions the balancing numbers scale the volumes directly. The 24 is needed only when a mass or an amount in moles is involved.

items.q: Carbon monoxide burns in oxygen: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide, both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?
items.why: The student picks up whichever balancing number is nearest, or scales in the direction that makes the number bigger, without tracking which species the number belongs to. Write the ratio with the species named: CO : O2 is 2 : 1, so the oxygen volume is half the carbon monoxide volume, 50 cm³.

items.q: Ethene burns completely: C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(l). 20 cm³ of ethene burns in excess oxygen. What volume of carbon dioxide is produced, measured at room temperature and pressure?
items.why: The rule 'one mole occupies 24 dm³' is remembered without the word 'gas', so it is applied to any substance in the equation whatever its state symbol. The molar volume of 24 dm³ applies to gases only. Read the state symbols and include only species labelled (g).

items.q: Two flasks of different gases at the same temperature and pressure hold the same volume. What must be equal about the two samples?
items.correct: The amounts in moles are equal.
items.misconception: Equal masses of two gases occupy equal volumes, so matching the masses matches the volumes.
items.why: Mass is the quantity students can see on a balance, and in earlier work 'how much' almost always meant mass, so mass is carried over as the quantity that must be matched. Volume is fixed by the amount in moles. 2 g of hydrogen and 2 g of oxygen are very different amounts in moles, so they occupy very different volumes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In what unit is the molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure given?
items.misconception: The size of the molar gas volume is remembered wrongly: the value 24 is given the wrong unit (24 cm3) or the wrong place value (e.g. 2.4 dm3), rather than 24 dm3 per mole.
items.why: Gas volumes in practical work are read off gas syringes in cm³, so cm³ becomes the automatic unit and the unit given in the specification is overwritten. The molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure is 24 dm³ per mole, which is 24 000 cm³ per mole. A gas syringe reading of 24 cm³ is only 0.001 mol.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 30 cm³ of nitrogen reacts fully. What volume of ammonia forms?
items.misconception: Gas volumes are conserved one for one, so 30 cm³ of a reactant gives 30 cm³ of a product.
items.why: Conservation of mass is a strong prior rule and gets transferred to volume, and the balancing numbers are read as decoration rather than as a ratio. Mass is conserved but the number of gas molecules is not. The balancing numbers give the volume ratio: 1 volume of N2 gives 2 volumes of NH3, so 30 cm³ gives 60 cm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.3.5 Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)
